orbital.title: Quantum Orbital Energy Diagram
orbital.subtitle: Aufbau subshell filling order & electron spins [↑↓]
orbital.aufbauDesc: Electrons fill lower-energy atomic orbitals (1s → 2s → 2p → 3s...) before filling higher-energy subshells to minimize total energy.
orbital.pauliDesc: No two electrons in an atom can have the same four quantum numbers. Each orbital holds at most 2 electrons with opposing spins (↑↓).
orbital.hundDesc: Degenerate orbitals of equal energy (e.g. 2px, 2py, 2pz) are each occupied by one electron with parallel spins (↑) before any orbital is paired up.

atomicRadius.name: Atomic Radius
atomicRadius.shortDescription: The typical distance from the center of the nucleus to the boundary of the surrounding electron cloud.
atomicRadius.studentExplanation: Atomic radius decreases across a period because the growing positive nuclear charge pulls valence electrons closer. It increases down a group because new electron shells are added.
atomicRadius.exceptionsExplanation: Noble gases are sometimes measured via van der Waals radius instead of covalent radius, making their values appear larger. Transition metal contraction also causes radii in period 5 and 6 to be very similar (lanthanide contraction).

ionizationEnergy.name: First Ionization Energy
ionizationEnergy.shortDescription: The energy required to remove the most loosely held electron from an isolated gaseous atom.
ionizationEnergy.studentExplanation: Ionization energy increases across a period as effective nuclear charge increases and atomic radius shrinks, holding valence electrons tighter. It decreases down a group as valence electrons sit in shells farther from the nucleus.
ionizationEnergy.exceptionsExplanation: Nitrogen has higher ionization energy than oxygen because nitrogen has a stable half-filled 2p³ subshell, whereas oxygen has a paired electron in 2p⁴ experiencing electron-electron repulsion. Similarly, beryllium (filled 2s²) has higher ionization energy than boron (2p¹).

electronegativity.name: Electronegativity
electronegativity.shortDescription: The relative ability of an atom in a chemical bond to attract shared electron pairs toward itself.
electronegativity.studentExplanation: Electronegativity increases across a period as nonmetals have high effective nuclear charge and want to gain electrons to complete octets. It decreases down a group due to increased shielding and distance from the nucleus.
electronegativity.exceptionsExplanation: Noble gases (He, Ne, Ar) generally lack Pauling electronegativity values because they do not readily form chemical bonds, though heavier noble gases like Kr and Xe form rare fluorides/oxides.

electronAffinity.name: Electron Affinity
electronAffinity.shortDescription: The amount of energy released when an electron is attached to a neutral gaseous atom to form an anion.
electronAffinity.studentExplanation: Generally becomes more exothermic across a period as atoms approach stable noble gas configurations. Halogens release the most energy upon gaining an electron.
electronAffinity.exceptionsExplanation: Chlorine has a higher electron affinity than fluorine because fluorine's tiny 2p subshell creates significant electron-electron repulsion that slightly destabilizes the incoming electron.

density.name: Density
density.shortDescription: Mass per unit volume of the element at standard temperature and pressure (STP).
density.studentExplanation: Density peaks in the middle of transition metals (periods 5 and 6) where atoms pack closely due to strong metallic bonding and high atomic masses in compact unit cells.
density.exceptionsExplanation: Osmium and Iridium are the densest naturally occurring elements (~22.6 g/cm³), nearly twice as dense as lead, due to the lanthanide contraction.

meltingPoint.name: Melting Point
meltingPoint.shortDescription: The temperature at which an element transitions from a solid to a liquid phase at standard atmospheric pressure.
meltingPoint.studentExplanation: Reflects the strength of interatomic bonding. Peaks around Group 6 (Cr, Mo, W) and carbon where maximum unpaired d-electrons or strong covalent network bonds exist.
meltingPoint.exceptionsExplanation: Tungsten (W) has the highest melting point of any metal (3695 K), while Carbon (diamond) sublimes above 3900 K. Conversely, Mercury is liquid at room temperature (234 K).

metallicCharacter.name: Metallic Character
metallicCharacter.shortDescription: The tendency of an element to lose electrons and exhibit typical metallic properties (conductivity, malleability, luster).
metallicCharacter.studentExplanation: Increases down a group and from right to left across a period, peaking at Francium/Cesium. Elements at the bottom-left lose valence electrons most easily.
metallicCharacter.exceptionsExplanation: The diagonal dividing line across the p-block contains metalloids (B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te) with intermediate properties.

help.bohrPara1: The 3D atom visualization utilizes an educational Bohr-style representation with concentric electron shells (K, L, M, N...) to help high-school and university students visualize electron distributions and valence shells.
help.bohrPara2: In modern quantum mechanics, electrons do not travel in fixed circular planetary tracks. Instead, they exist in three-dimensional probability wave distributions (orbitals: s, p, d, f) dictated by the Schrödinger wave equation and the Heisenberg uncertainty principle.
